newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: French influence wanes in former colony Cambodia. [CORRECTED 08:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: French influence wanes in former colony Cambodia. [CORRECTED 08:50 GMT]

text.p: Cambodia celebrates 43 years of independence from French rule on Saturday as a young generation and most of its leaders look to new, English-speaking friends to guide them into the 21st century, analysts say.
Bread rolls, cafe au lait, elegant villas on spacious boulevards and battered old Peugeots are among the legacies of French rule from 1863 to 1953 (corrects from 1864 to 1953).

France remains an important and generous friend to Cambodia, but its dominating influence of the 1950s and 1960s has waned, especially the use of the French language, despite the efforts of francophones to stem the trend.
"It's because we've been away for a long time, between 1975 and '91...that was enough to reduce our influence, especially as long as the former elite had been destroyed," a French diplomat said.
He was refering to the 1975-79 "killing fields" years of Khmer Rouge rule during which more than a million Cambodians died from starvation, disease, overwork and execution.
The Khmer Rouge launched a catastrophic programme of radical agrarian reform that targeted intellectuals and professionals, most of whom spoke French, for execution.
Vietnam invaded Cambodia at the end of 1978 and for the next 13 years the country was gripped by guerrilla war. It remained isolated until a U.N. peace treaty was signed in 1991 in Paris.
French and Cambodian officials acknowledge that the countries of the region, the most dynamic in the world, are today's role models for the Indochina nation.

"We are surrounded by countries that use English," said Public Works and Transport Minister Ing Kieth, a veteran civil servant with a French background and a member of the cabinet introduced to the late French President Charles de Gaulle on his 1966 visit.

Observers said Cambodia was due to join its neighbours as a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) next year, and noted its main investment and trade partners came from Asia and used English as a working medium.
Few support the views of Cambodia's top francophone, King Norodom Sihanouk, who has said French should be promoted as the first foreign language as it "neutralises Anglo-Saxon and ASEAN influences".

"The young generation now, they want to study English and Cambodia will become a member of ASEAN," said MP Ahmad Yahya, who drives one of the ubiquitous workhorses of the provinces, an old French Peugeot.

Sebastien Drans, deputy editor of the French-language Cambodge Soir, said that while his newpaper's circulation was small and subsidised, it reached an elite readership. He also noted that French television and radio were still broadcast.
But university students, including many who must study in French, believe English is the passport to a prosperous future in a country where few major French firms have dared to invest.

Most French are pragmatic about their chances of turning back the clock -- President Jacques Chirac has publicly supported Cambodia's bid to join ASEAN -- but they seem determined to maintain an important role and presence.

About 2,000 French live in the country, and France's biggest cultural centre in Asia is in Phnom Penh. Paris is one of the top three donors with $50 million in civil aid and $5 million in military aid earmarked for 1996.
The lion's share of the aid is headed for education, followed by health and rural development, the diplomat said.
"The French are helping us a lot," said MP Yahya. "But I don't think they can influence Cambodia like before."
